analogy.p: Picture the nucleus as a tiny marble at the centre spot of a football stadium, with the electrons like specks of dust flying around the outer stands. Almost all the weight is in the marble, and almost all of the volume is empty space, just like an atom. Isotopes are marbles with the same number of red (proton) beads but different numbers of grey (neutron) beads. The analogy breaks down because electrons are not tiny solid balls on set paths and the real scale is even more extreme: the atom is 100 000 times wider than the nucleus.
analogy.t: A tiny marble in a huge stadium

bullets: The nucleus is at the centre and is positively charged because protons are positive and neutrons are neutral.
Electrons orbit in energy levels (shells) around the nucleus and are held by the electrostatic attraction between negative electrons and the positive nucleus.
Nearly all the mass of an atom is concentrated in its nucleus because protons and neutrons are much heavier than electrons.
Most of the volume of an atom is empty space, which is why most alpha particles pass straight through gold foil in the scattering experiment.
Atoms are electrically neutral overall: the number of protons equals the number of electrons.
Link to other topics: the arrangement of electrons controls chemical bonding and the position of an element in the periodic table.
core.h: The nuclear model of the atom
core.p: Atoms are the tiny particles that make up all matter. In the modern **nuclear model** an atom has a very small, dense, positively charged **nucleus** at its centre, surrounded by negatively charged **electrons** that occupy energy levels (shells) at different distances from the nucleus. Almost all of the mass of the atom is in the nucleus, but the nucleus takes up only a tiny fraction of the atom's volume, so most of an atom is empty space. The nucleus contains **protons** and **neutrons**, which are together called nucleons.

bullets: Radius of an atom ≈ 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m.
Radius of the nucleus is less than 1/10 000 of the atom's radius (about 1 × 10⁻¹⁵ m).
Ratio of atom radius to nucleus radius = (1 × 10⁻¹⁰) ÷ (1 × 10⁻¹⁵) = 1 × 10⁵ = 100 000.
Standard form uses powers of 10: 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ means 0.0000000001 m.
Although the nucleus is tiny, it contains over 99.9% of the atom's mass.
These sizes are far too small to see with a light microscope, so they were found from scattering experiments.
core.h: Size of the atom and the nucleus
core.p: An atom has a radius of about **1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m** (0.1 nanometres). The radius of the nucleus is less than **1/10 000** of the radius of the atom, which is about 1 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. This means the atom is around 100 000 times wider than its nucleus. If an atom were scaled up to the size of a large stadium, the nucleus would be about the size of a pinhead in the centre. You should be able to use standard form for these sizes and do simple comparisons.

bullets: **Proton**: relative charge +1, relative mass 1, found in the nucleus.
**Neutron**: relative charge 0 (neutral), relative mass 1, found in the nucleus.
**Electron**: relative charge −1, relative mass very small, found in energy levels outside the nucleus.
Protons and neutrons have almost the same mass, which is why the mass number is found by adding them.
The electron mass is so small that it is ignored when calculating the mass number.
The charges of a proton and an electron are equal in size but opposite, so equal numbers make an atom neutral.
core.h: Protons, neutrons and electrons: relative charge and mass
core.p: The three sub-atomic particles are compared using **relative** values, because the real masses and charges are very small numbers. A proton has relative charge +1 and relative mass 1, a neutron has relative charge 0 and relative mass 1, and an electron has relative charge −1 and a relative mass that is very small (about 1/1836 of a proton). Learning this table is essential because mark schemes ask for it directly.

bullets: Atomic number (Z) = number of protons.
Mass number (A) = number of protons + number of neutrons.
Number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
In a neutral atom, number of electrons = number of protons = atomic number.
The periodic table is arranged in order of increasing atomic number.
Mass number is always a whole number; relative atomic mass on the periodic table is an average and is not.
core.p: The **atomic number** is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom, and it defines which element the atom is. All atoms of the same element have the same atomic number, and a different atomic number means a different element. The **mass number** is the total number of protons and neutrons (nucleons) in the nucleus. The number of neutrons is therefore found by subtracting: neutrons = mass number − atomic number.

bullets: Top number = mass number (nucleons).
Bottom number = atomic number (protons).
¹⁴₆C: 6 protons, 14 − 6 = 8 neutrons, 6 electrons if neutral.
The symbol and the atomic number give the same information, but both are normally written.
The 'carbon-14' form gives the mass number, so you must find the atomic number from the periodic table.
In nuclear equations (later topic) the top and bottom numbers must balance on each side.
core.p: Atoms are written using a symbol with two numbers: the mass number at the top left and the atomic number at the bottom left, for example ¹⁴₆C for carbon-14. The chemical symbol tells you the element, the bottom number tells you the protons, and the top number tells you the total of protons and neutrons. Isotopes can also be written in words, such as carbon-14, where the number is the mass number.

bullets: Definition (mark scheme style): atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
Carbon-12 has 6 neutrons; carbon-13 has 7; carbon-14 has 8, all with 6 protons.
Same electron arrangement → same chemical reactions.
Different mass → slightly different physical properties, such as density.
Some isotopes are unstable and radioactive, such as carbon-14 and uranium-235.
Isotopes of one element share a name and an atomic number but differ in mass number.
core.p: **Isotopes** are atoms of the same element, so they have the same number of protons, but a different number of neutrons. They therefore have the same atomic number but different mass numbers. Isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties because chemistry depends on the electron arrangement, which is determined by the number of protons. They differ in mass and, for some, in whether the nucleus is stable or radioactive.

bullets: Step 1: compare atomic numbers; if different, they are different elements.
Step 2: if atomic numbers are the same, compare mass numbers.
Same atomic number, different mass number = isotopes.
Same mass number, different atomic number = different elements (not isotopes).
Neutrons have no charge so they cannot change the electron arrangement.
Many elements exist as mixtures of isotopes, which is why relative atomic masses are not whole numbers.
core.h: Why isotopes are the same element
core.p: The identity of an element is set by the number of protons, so changing the number of neutrons does not change the element. Neutrons add mass and affect nuclear stability, but have no charge, so they do not affect how the atom bonds with others. A common exam question asks you to compare two atoms and decide whether they are isotopes, so the method is to compare protons first and neutrons second.

bullets: Energy levels are at different distances from the nucleus.
Lower level = closer to nucleus = less energy; higher level = further away = more energy.
Electrons fill the lowest available energy levels first.
The outermost electrons are held least strongly, so they are the ones most easily lost.
Only specific energy changes are possible, so only specific frequencies are absorbed or emitted.
This is the basis of line spectra used to identify elements.
core.p: Electrons occupy fixed **energy levels** (shells) at different distances from the nucleus. An electron in a lower level is closer to the nucleus and has less energy, while one in a higher level is further away and has more energy. The electrons are in the lowest available levels in an atom in its normal state, and the arrangement can change when the atom interacts with electromagnetic radiation. This idea explains why atoms emit and absorb only certain wavelengths of light.

bullets: Absorb EM radiation → electron moves up to a higher energy level.
Electron falls to a lower level → emits EM radiation.
Absorbed or emitted energy matches the energy difference between the levels.
Larger energy gap → higher frequency (and shorter wavelength) of radiation.
An atom with an electron in a higher level is said to be excited.
Higher tier idea: an electron can only absorb radiation if its energy matches a possible jump.
core.h: Absorption and emission of electromagnetic radiation
core.p: When an atom absorbs **electromagnetic radiation** of the right energy, an electron can move to a higher energy level, further from the nucleus. When the electron falls back to a lower energy level, the atom **emits** electromagnetic radiation. The frequency of the radiation depends on the size of the energy change, so bigger energy gaps give higher frequencies. This is the source of the light emitted by heated gases and of flame test colours.

bullets: Atom loses outer electron(s) → positive ion (more protons than electrons).
Atom gains electron(s) → negative ion.
Na → Na⁺ + e⁻: sodium has 11 protons and 11 electrons, so Na⁺ has 11 protons and 10 electrons.
Only electrons move; protons are fixed in the nucleus, so the atomic number stays the same.
Ionising radiation (alpha, beta, gamma) can knock electrons out of atoms, making ions.
Ionisation is why radiation is dangerous to living cells.
core.p: If an atom loses or gains electrons it becomes an **ion**, which has an overall electric charge. Outer electrons can be removed from an atom when it absorbs enough energy, for example from ionising radiation or high temperatures. Losing electrons leaves more protons than electrons, so the ion has a positive charge, whereas gaining electrons gives a negative ion. The number of protons does not change, so the element stays the same.

bullets: Neutral atom: protons = electrons.
Positive ion with charge +n: electrons = protons − n.
Negative ion with charge −n: electrons = protons + n.
Isotopes: protons are equal; neutrons are different.
Neutrons are never affected by ionisation because they are in the nucleus.
Example: ²³₁₁Na⁺ has 11 protons, 12 neutrons, 10 electrons.
core.p: It helps to compare atoms, ions and isotopes in one place because exam questions often ask you to work out numbers of particles. For any particle you can find the protons from the atomic number, the neutrons from the mass number, and the electrons from the charge. Practising this with a table makes it automatic.

bullets: Most alpha particles passed straight through → atom is mostly empty space.
Some were deflected → there is a positive charge in the nucleus repelling positive alpha particles.
A few bounced straight back → the nucleus is very small and dense.
This replaced the plum pudding model, which had no nucleus.
Later Bohr suggested electrons orbit at fixed distances (energy levels).
Chadwick's discovery of the neutron explained why mass number is larger than atomic number.
core.h: Development of ideas and evidence for the nuclear model
core.p: Our picture of the atom came from experiments. Scientists found that most alpha particles fired at thin gold foil went straight through, a few were deflected through large angles and a very few bounced back. This shows that the atom is mostly empty space with a small, dense, positively charged nucleus. This history is covered in detail in the next spec point, but you should know it supports the size and structure given here.

bullets: Isotopes → used in radioactive decay and half-life.
Ionisation → why alpha is the most ionising radiation.
Energy levels → emission and absorption of radiation, including infrared and visible light.
Electron arrangement → chemical bonding (chemistry link).
Standard form → needed to compare atom and nucleus sizes.
Always state the relative charge with its sign: +1, 0, −1.
core.p: Atomic structure underpins the whole of Paper 1 radioactivity and links to chemistry. In physics exams you may be asked to count particles, define isotopes, explain ionisation, or describe energy-level changes. Combining these with the nuclear equation topic, you must always check that top numbers and bottom numbers balance. Use the correct terms: 'nucleus', 'proton', 'electron', not 'centre' or 'particle'.

exam: Learn the relative charge and mass table exactly: proton +1 and 1; neutron 0 and 1; electron −1 and very small.
1 mark questions: definitions such as 'atomic number = number of protons' or 'isotopes = same protons, different neutrons'.
2 mark counting questions: give protons (atomic number), neutrons (mass − atomic number) and electrons, each shown clearly.
For isotopes, state both parts: 'same number of protons' AND 'different number of neutrons'. One part alone scores 1 of 2.
For ions, explain in terms of electrons only: 'lost one electron so more protons than electrons, giving a +1 charge'.
For energy levels, use the exact phrases: 'absorbs electromagnetic radiation', 'moves to a higher energy level', 'emits electromagnetic radiation' when it falls.
Size questions: quote 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m for the atom and say the nucleus radius is less than 1/10 000 of this; be able to do a ratio in standard form.
4 mark 'explain' questions on structure: nucleus is small and dense and positive, electrons in energy levels, mass concentrated in nucleus, atom neutral because protons = electrons.
Check numbers: neutrons cannot be negative, and the mass number must be larger than or equal to the atomic number.
Show working for neutron counts (mass number − atomic number) so you can pick up method marks.

mistakes.r: Isotopes have the same number of protons (same atomic number) but a different number of neutrons.
mistakes.w: Isotopes have a different number of protons.

mistakes.r: The mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons; the atomic number is the number of protons.
mistakes.w: The mass number is the number of protons.

mistakes.r: Electrons are in energy levels (shells) outside the nucleus.
Isotopes have the same chemical properties because they have the same number of electrons (same electron arrangement).
An atom becomes an ion by gaining or losing electrons; the protons stay in the nucleus.
mistakes.w: An atom becomes an ion by gaining or losing protons.

mistakes.r: A neutron has relative mass 1 and relative charge 0.
mistakes.w: A neutron has a relative mass of 0 (as it has no charge).

mistakes.r: An electron has a very small mass (not zero), relative charge −1.
The nucleus is tiny (radius less than 1/10 000 of the atom) but contains almost all of the mass.
mistakes.w: The nucleus is the biggest part of the atom.

mistakes.r: Electrons absorb electromagnetic radiation and move to a higher energy level, further from the nucleus.
mistakes.w: Electrons absorb energy and move closer to the nucleus.

summary: You must know the size and structure of an atom, the relative charge and mass of protons, neutrons and electrons, and how atomic number and mass number describe an atom. You must also explain what isotopes are, how atoms become ions, and how electrons can move between energy levels by absorbing or emitting electromagnetic radiation. This is the foundation for all of atomic physics, radioactivity and the periodic table.

terms.d: The smallest part of an element that can exist; it has a nucleus surrounded by electrons and no overall charge.
The small, dense, positively charged centre of an atom containing protons and neutrons.
A positively charged particle in the nucleus with relative charge +1 and relative mass 1.
A particle in the nucleus with no charge (0) and relative mass 1.
A negatively charged particle with relative charge −1 and very small mass that moves in energy levels outside the nucleus.
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.
A particle found in the nucleus; either a proton or a neutron.
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
A substance made of atoms that all have the same number of protons.
An atom or group of atoms with an overall electric charge because it has lost or gained electrons.
A fixed position (shell) at a particular distance from the nucleus that an electron can occupy.
Waves that transfer energy and can be absorbed or emitted by atoms when electrons change energy level.
The process of an atom losing one or more electrons to form a positive ion.
A way of writing very large or small numbers as a number between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of 10.

worked.ans: (a) 11 protons, 12 neutrons, 11 electrons. (b) 11 protons, 12 neutrons, 10 electrons.
worked.q: A sodium atom is written as ²³₁₁Na. State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in (a) a neutral atom and (b) a Na⁺ ion. (4 marks)
steps: (b) Na⁺ has lost one electron: electrons = 11 − 1 = 10; protons (11) and neutrons (12) unchanged.

worked.ans: U-235 has 143 neutrons and U-238 has 146. They are isotopes because they have the same number of protons (92) but a different number of neutrons.
worked.q: Uranium-235 (atomic number 92) and uranium-238 are isotopes. Calculate the number of neutrons in each and explain why they are isotopes. (4 marks)
steps: Both have 92 protons, so the same atomic number and same element.
The numbers of neutrons differ (143 and 146), so they are isotopes.

worked.ans: The atom's radius is 100 000 (1 × 10⁵) times bigger than the nucleus. The nucleus is a tiny fraction of the atom's volume, so most of the atom is empty space, but most of the mass is in the nucleus.
worked.q: The radius of an atom is 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m and the radius of its nucleus is 1 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. How many times bigger is the radius of the atom than the radius of the nucleus? Then explain what this shows about the atom. (3 marks)
steps: The nucleus is tiny compared with the atom, so most of the atom is empty space.
